claim: Recent studies suggest that the cross-sectional relationship between reading skills and white matter microstructure, as indexed by fractional anisotropy, is not as robust as previously thought.
source: Recent studies suggest that the cross-sectional relationship between reading skills and white matter microstructure, as indexed by fractional anisotropy, is not as robust as previously thought.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to other studies in the manuscript, as indicated by the reference to 'recent studies' and is further elaborated in the introduction section.

claim: Fixel-based analyses yield fiber-specific micro- and macrostructural measures, overcoming several shortcomings of the traditional diffusion tensor model.
source: Fixel-based analyses yield fiber-specific micro- and macrostructural measures, overcoming several shortcomings of the traditional diffusion tensor model.
evidence: This claim is supported by knowledge about fixel-based analysis methods and their advantages over DTI, as described in the introduction.

claim: The study analyzed 983 children and adolescents ages 6–18 from a large, open, quality-controlled dataset.
source: We ran a whole-brain analysis investigating whether the product of fiber density and cross-section (FDC) related to single-word reading skills in a large, open, quality-controlled dataset of 983 children and adolescents ages 6–18.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the participant data described in the results section.

claim: FDC positively related to reading skills throughout the brain, especially in left temporoparietal and cerebellar white matter.
source: We found that FDC positively related to reading skills throughout the brain, especially in left temporoparietal and cerebellar white matter, but did not differ between reading proficiency groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in Figure 3 and described in the results section.

claim: FDC did not differ between participants with (n = 102) and without (n = 570) reading disabilities.
source: We found that FDC positively related to reading skills throughout the brain, especially in left temporoparietal and cerebellar white matter, but did not differ between reading proficiency groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis comparing the TR and RD groups as described in the results.

claim: Among metrics from other diffusion models, only the orientation dispersion and neurite density indexes from NODDI were associated (inversely) with reading skills.
source: Exploratory analyses revealed that among metrics from other diffusion models – diffusion tensor imaging, diffusion kurtosis imaging, and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging – only the orientation dispersion and neurite density indexes from NODDI were associated (inversely) with reading skills.
evidence: This claim is supported by the exploratory analysis results presented in Figure 4 and described in the results section.

claim: FA is a metric derived from the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) model that quantifies the degree to which water diffusion is directionally restricted in each voxel.
source: FA is a metric derived from the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) model (Basser et al., 1994) that quantifies the degree to which water diffusion is directionally restricted in each voxel (Hagmann et al., 2006; Basser and Pierpaoli, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational DTI literature.

claim: FA is high in white matter compared with gray matter and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) due to preferential water movement along the axis of axons.
source: FA is high in white matter compared with gray matter and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) due to preferential water movement along the axis of axons.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about water diffusion in brain tissue.

claim: FA is prone to partial volume effects, manifesting as reduced FA in regions where white matter borders gray matter or CSF.
source: As a metric defined on the voxel-level, FA is prone to partial volume effects, manifesting as reduced FA in regions where white matter borders gray matter or CSF (Vos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vos et al., 2011.

claim: FA is artificially lower in regions of crossing fibers, affecting up to 90% of white matter voxels.
source: Due to the limited degrees of freedom in the tensor model, FA is artificially lower in regions of crossing fibers, affecting up to 90% of white matter voxels (Behrens et al., 2007; Jeurissen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Behrens et al., 2007 and Jeurissen et al., 2013.

claim: FA tends to covary with multiple elements such as axonal diameter, density, permeability, and coherence.
source: In addition to sensitivity to myelination, FA also tends to covary with other elements such as axonal diameter, density, permeability, and coherence (Beaulieu, 2009; Johansen-Berg and Behrens, 2013; Shemesh, 2018; Friedrich et al., 2020; Lazari and Lipp, 2021), and information from DTI alone is not sufficient to gauge the individual contributions of these features.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing the complexity of FA interpretation.

claim: Early cross-sectional studies of FA and reading skills seemed to converge towards a consensus of greater FA relating to better reading ability, particularly in left temporoparietal white matter tracts.
source: Early cross-sectional studies of FA and reading skills seemed to converge towards a consensus of greater FA relating to better reading ability, particularly in left temporoparietal white matter tracts that connect neocortical regions known to be important for language, such as the arcuate fasciculus (AF) and superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) (Klingberg et al., 2000; Ben et al., 2007; Vandermosten et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to early studies in the field.

claim: Subsequent studies began describing a range of results including significant FA-reading relationships in different areas and regions where higher FA was associated with worse reading skills.
source: As tract segmentation algorithms became more robust and widely used, subsequent studies, empowered to address tract-specific hypotheses, began describing a range of results. These included significant FA-reading relationships in different areas, such as commissural (Frye et al., 2008; Lebel et al., 2013), cerebellar (Travis et al., 2015; Bruckert et al., 2020), and right-lateralized bundles (Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2015), as well as regions where higher FA was associated with worse reading skills (Carter et al., 2009; Frye et al., 2011; Christodoulou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing varied results.

claim: A meta-analysis of whole-brain voxel-based studies found no regions where FA either varied with reading ability or was reduced in dyslexic compared with typically reading individuals.
source: A meta-analysis of whole-brain voxel-based studies found no regions where FA either varied with reading ability or was reduced in dyslexic compared with typically reading, individuals (Moreau et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moreau et al., 2018.

claim: Three large-scale cross-sectional studies using publicly available datasets found largely null associations between FA and reading skills in several tracts.
source: Three large-scale cross-sectional studies using publicly available datasets found largely null associations between FA and reading skills in several tracts (Koirala et al., 2021; Meisler and Gabrieli, 2022; Roy et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three recent large-scale studies.

claim: Reading involves the functioning of a widely distributed brain network.
source: Reading involves the functioning of a widely distributed brain network (Cattinelli et al., 2013; Wandell and Yeatman, 2013; Murphy et al., 2019), and white matter tracts are conduits for information sent within this network (Ben et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing the reading network.

claim: Lesion-mapping analyses and clinical case studies have demonstrated that white matter connections, primarily in the left hemisphere, are necessary for reading.
source: Lesion-mapping analyses (Wang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021) and clinical case studies (Epelbaum et al., 2008; Rauschecker et al., 2009) have demonstrated that white matter connections, primarily in the left hemisphere, are necessary for reading.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to lesion-mapping and case study literature.

claim: White matter exhibits learning-driven plasticity and can modulate neuronal firing patterns.
source: Since white matter exhibits learning-driven plasticity and can also modulate neuronal firing patterns (Fields, 2015; Xin and Chan, 2020), one may expect that functional variation, such as differences in reading ability, may be reflected by some white matter structural property (Ramus et al., 2018; Protopapas and Parrila, 2018; Protopapas and Parrila, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on white matter plasticity.

claim: Fixel-based analyses perform statistical inferences on 'fixels,' or individual fiber populations within voxels, using three fixel-derived metrics: fiber density (FD), fiber cross-section (FC), and their product (FDC).
source: Subsequently, a DWI analytical paradigm was introduced that performs statistical inferences on 'fixels,' or individual fiber populations within voxels, using a set of three fixel-derived metrics: fiber density (FD), fiber cross-section (FC), and their product (FDC) (Raffelt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Raffelt et al., 2015, which introduced the fixel-based analysis framework.

claim: FD is a microstructural measure that reflects the intra-axonal volume fraction.
source: FD is a microstructural measure that reflects the intra-axonal volume fraction (Raffelt et al., 2012b; Genc et al., 2020), while FC is a macrostructural measure related to the cross-sectional area of fiber bundles (Raffelt et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raffelt et al., 2012b and Genc et al., 2020.

claim: FC is a macrostructural measure related to the cross-sectional area of fiber bundles.
source: FD is a microstructural measure that reflects the intra-axonal volume fraction (Raffelt et al., 2012b; Genc et al., 2020), while FC is a macrostructural measure related to the cross-sectional area of fiber bundles (Raffelt et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Raffelt et al., 2012b.

claim: FDC is related to the total estimated intra-axonal volume and is sensitive to both white matter micro- and macrostructure.
source: The product of FD and FC, or FDC, is therefore related to the total estimated intra-axonal volume and is sensitive to both white matter micro- and macrostructure.
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical relationship between FD and FC and their biological interpretations.

claim: Wider axons conduct action potentials more quickly and can fire more often at their terminals.
source: Wider axons conduct action potentials more quickly and can fire more often at their terminals (Perge et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perge et al., 2012.

claim: FDC is thought to more closely relate to the conductive capacity of white matter.
source: Thus, FDC is thought to more closely relate to the conductive capacity of white matter (Raffelt et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Raffelt et al., 2017b and inference from the properties of FDC.

claim: FBAs are by nature restricted to white matter, thus mitigating the effects of multiple comparison correction from redundant regions in other neural compartments.
source: Since FBAs operate on the level of fixels, and fixels are generated from FODs in white matter, FBAs are by nature restricted to white matter, thus mitigating the effects of multiple comparison correction from redundant regions in other neural compartments.
evidence: This claim is based on the methodology of fixel-based analysis as described in the introduction.

claim: Spatial smoothing in FBAs is performed within local neighborhoods of white matter bundles informed by fixel connectivity.
source: Spatial smoothing in FBAs is performed within local neighborhoods of white matter bundles informed by fixel connectivity (Raffelt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Raffelt et al., 2015.

claim: The signal in a given fixel is not influenced by different tissue classes or other fiber populations, in contrast to traditional voxel-based spatial smoothing.
source: Thus, the signal in a given fixel is not influenced by different tissue classes or other fiber populations, in contrast to traditional voxel-based spatial smoothing, which operates more indiscriminately.
evidence: This claim is based on the comparison between fixel-based and voxel-based smoothing methods.

claim: The 983 participants who passed all inclusion, exclusion, and quality control criteria were divided into a typically reading group (TR; n = 570) and reading disability group (RD; n = 102).
source: The 983 participants who passed all inclusion, exclusion, and quality control criteria (Table 1) were divided into a typically reading group (TR; n = 570) and reading disability group (RD; n = 102) based on diagnostic and standardized reading assessments (Figure 2; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results section and supported by Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: A total of 311 participants did not meet the criteria for either group, but were still included in the correlation analyses.
source: A total of 311 participants did not meet the criteria for either group, but were still included in the correlation analyses.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results section.

claim: The TR group, compared with the RD group, was older and had higher socioeconomic scores, brain volumes, verbal IQ, visuospatial IQ, age-normalized reading scores, globally averaged fixel metrics, and image quality.
source: The TR group, compared with the RD group, was older and had higher socioeconomic scores, brain volumes, verbal IQ, visuospatial IQ, age-normalized reading scores, globally averaged fixel metrics, and image quality (as indexed by the average neighbor correlation; see Yeh et al., 2019 for more information on this metric).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: The TR and RD groups were matched in sex distribution, handedness, and average motion (mean framewise displacement).
source: The groups were matched in sex distribution (although the cohort as a whole was male-skewed), handedness, and average motion (mean framewise displacement).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: There were no appreciable clusters in which an inverse relationship between FDC and reading skills was observed.
source: There were no appreciable clusters in which an inverse relationship between FDC and reading skills was observed.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis results described in the results section.

claim: Each tract produced by the segmentation software, TractSeg, contained significant fixels.
source: Each tract produced by the segmentation software, TractSeg (Wasserthal et al., 2018a), contained significant fixels (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Table 2.

claim: The effect size of significant fixels varied up to a peak value of 0.030.
source: The effect size of significant fixels varied up to a peak value of 0.030.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results section.

claim: The temporoparietal cluster was most likely associated with the left arcuate fasciculus (AF), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), or middle longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).
source: Tract segmentation intersections (Table 2) revealed that the temporoparietal cluster was most likely associated with the left arcuate fasciculus (AF), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), or middle longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).
evidence: This claim is based on tract segmentation analysis results presented in Table 2.

claim: The cerebellar cluster was most likely associated with the left superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP).
source: The cerebellar cluster was most likely associated with the left superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP).
evidence: This claim is based on tract segmentation analysis results.

claim: Homotopic clusters of significant fixels were observed in right-hemisphere temporoparietal and cerebellar white matter, but they reached smaller effect sizes than those in the left hemisphere.
source: Homotopic clusters of significant fixels were observed in right-hemisphere temporoparietal and cerebellar white matter, but they reached smaller effect sizes than those in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis results described in the results section.

claim: Post-hoc exploration revealed that among metrics, better reading skills were associated with higher FC compared with fewer regions where higher FD was related to better reading.
source: Post-hoc exploration of FD and FC revealed diffuse associations of better reading skills with higher FC compared with fewer regions where higher FD was related to better reading (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the post-hoc analysis results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Highest effect sizes of FDC were achieved in regions where higher FD and FC were both independently related with better reading.
source: As expected, highest effect sizes of FDC were achieved in regions where higher FD and FC were both independently related with better reading.
evidence: This claim is based on the post-hoc analysis results and the mathematical relationship between FDC, FD, and FC.

claim: No significant differences in FDC were found between the TR and RD groups.
source: We did not find any significant differences in FDC between the TR and RD groups.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results section.

claim: Only two trivially small clusters (consisting of one and seven fixels) showed age-related variance in FDC-TOWRE relationships.
source: Only two trivially small clusters (consisting of one and seven fixels) showed age-related variance in FDC-TOWRE relationships.
evidence: This claim is based on the bivariate interaction model results described in the results section.

claim: The relationship between FDC and reading skills was stable across ages.
source: These small clusters did not intersect with significant fixels from the primary analysis, suggesting that the relationship between FDC and reading skills was stable across ages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the bivariate interaction model results.

claim: Metrics from DTI (FA and mean diffusivity [MD]) and DKI (kurtosis fractional anisotropy [KFA] and mean kurtosis [MK]) did not relate to reading skills.
source: We found that metrics from DTI (FA and mean diffusivity [MD]) and DKI (kurtosis fractional anisotropy [KFA] and mean kurtosis [MK]) did not relate to reading skills.
evidence: This claim is based on the exploratory analysis results described in the results section.

claim: For ODI, the regions of highest effect sizes overlapped with the left temporoparietal and bilateral cerebellar regions that were significant in the primary analysis of FDC.
source: For ODI, the regions of highest effect sizes overlapped with the left temporoparietal and bilateral cerebellar regions that were significant in the primary analysis of FDC.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the ODI and FDC analysis results.

claim: Clusters in neither of the NODDI models survived multiple comparison correction across hypotheses (Bonferroni factor of 12).
source: Clusters in neither of the NODDI models survived multiple comparison correction across hypotheses (Bonferroni factor of 12).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results section.

claim: The AF and SLF connect inferior frontal and temporoparietal gray matter regions that are essential for language and reading processing.
source: The AF and SLF connect inferior frontal and temporoparietal gray matter regions that are essential for language and reading processing (Catani et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Catani et al., 2005.

claim: Lesion symptom mapping studies have demonstrated that the AF and SLF are vital connections in the reading network.
source: Lesion symptom mapping studies have demonstrated that the AF and SLF are vital connections in the reading network (Baldo et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baldo et al., 2018 and Li et al., 2021.

claim: These tracts, particularly in the left hemisphere, are associated with phonological processing skills, which are critical to reading and impaired in dyslexia.
source: These tracts, particularly in the left hemisphere, are associated with phonological processing skills (Yeatman et al., 2011), which are critical to reading (Vellutino and Scanlon, 1987) and impaired in dyslexia (Swan and Goswami, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on phonological processing and reading.

claim: Longitudinal studies have suggested that ventral tracts (IFOF and ILF) are more associated with visual orthographic, as opposed to phonological, processing.
source: Longitudinal studies have suggested that these ventral tracts are more associated with visual orthographic, as opposed to phonological, processing (Yeatman et al., 2012; Vanderauwera et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yeatman et al., 2012 and Vanderauwera et al., 2018.

claim: Phonological skills, as opposed to lower-level visual and orthographic processing, may provide more of a bottleneck to single-word reading abilities in children.
source: Our results suggest that phonological skills, as opposed to lower-level visual and orthographic processing, may provide more of a bottleneck to single-word reading abilities in children.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of results showing stronger effects in dorsal vs. ventral tracts.

claim: The SCP contains efferent fibers that connect deep cerebellar nuclei to contralateral thalamic cortical regions.
source: In particular, the SCP contains efferent fibers that connect deep cerebellar nuclei to contralateral thalamic cortical regions.
evidence: This claim is based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Co-activation of language-dominant hemispheric inferior frontal regions and contralateral cerebellar regions during verbal tasks suggests that the SCP may be a putative tract for cortico-cerebellar interactions in verbal processing.
source: Co-activation of language-dominant hemispheric inferior frontal regions and contralateral cerebellar regions during verbal tasks (Jansen et al., 2005) suggests that the SCP may be a putative tract for cortico-cerebellar interactions in verbal processing.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited functional imaging data.

claim: Previous studies have reported that FA of bilateral SCP inversely relates to reading skills.
source: Previous studies have reported that FA of bilateral SCP inversely relates to reading skills (Travis et al., 2015; Bruckert et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Travis et al., 2015 and Bruckert et al., 2020.

claim: The study did not find an inverse relationship between FDC and reading abilities in the SCP.
source: We did not find an inverse relationship between FDC and reading abilities, although one should not a priori expect FA and FDC to covary.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the discussion section.

claim: Approximately 50% of children with reading disorders also qualify for a diagnosis of ADHD.
source: Such co-occurring difficulties occur at high rates in reading disorders; for example, approximately 50% of children with reading disorders also qualify for a diagnosis of ADHD (Willcutt et al., 2010; DuPaul et al., 2013; Al Dahhan et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Willcutt et al., 2010, DuPaul et al., 2013, and Al Dahhan et al., 2022.

claim: The b-value of 2000 s/mm² is not exceptionally large compared to the spectrum of values typically employed in FBA.
source: The b-value of 2000 s/mm2, while higher than the b-value of typical DTI acquisitions, is not exceptionally large compared to the spectrum of values typically employed in FBA.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of typical FBA acquisition parameters.

claim: Measures of FD, and therefore FDC, may have been partially undermined by contamination from extra-axonal signal due to the b-value used.
source: Thus, our measures of FD, and therefore FDC as well, may have been partially undermined by contamination from extra-axonal signal (Genc et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the b-value used and citation to Genc et al., 2020.

claim: Data were collected using either a 1.5T Siemens mobile scanner (Staten Island site) or a 3T Siemens MRI scanner (sites at Rutgers University Brain Imaging Center, Cornell Brain Imaging Center, and the City University of New York Advanced Science Research Center).
source: Data were collected using either a 1.5T Siemens mobile scanner (Staten Island site) or a 3T Siemens MRI scanner (sites at Rutgers University Brain Imaging Center, Cornell Brain Imaging Center, and the City University of New York Advanced Science Research Center).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A DKI scan was acquired with 1.8 mm isotropic voxel resolution, 1 b = 0 s/mm² image, and 64 noncollinear directions collected at b = 1000 s/mm² and b = 2000 s/mm².
source: A DKI scan was acquired with 1.8 mm isotropic voxel resolution, 1 b = 0 s/mm2 image, and 64 noncollinear directions collected at b = 1000 s/mm2 and b = 2000 s/mm2.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A total of 102 participants were diagnosed with a 'specific learning disability with impairment in reading' following the 5th edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual for Mental Disorders and scored ≤ 85 on both TOWRE subtests (age-standardized).
source: A total of 102 participants were diagnosed with a 'specific learning disability with impairment in reading; following the 5th edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual for Mental Disorders (Edition, 2013) and scored ≤ 85 on both TOWRE subtests (age-standardized).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A total of 570 participants who were not diagnosed with a reading impairment and scored ≥ 90 on both TOWRE subtests (age-standardized) were placed in the TR group.
source: A total of 570 participants who were not diagnosed with a reading impairment and scored ≥ 90 on both TOWRE subtests (age-standardized) were placed in the TR group.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Response functions for white matter, gray matter, and CSF were estimated with MRtrix3's unsupervised dhollander algorithm.
source: Response functions for white matter, gray matter, and CSF were estimated with MRtrix3's unsupervised dhollander algorithm (Dhollander et al., 2016; Dhollander et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Site-specific average fiber response functions were calculated across participants to enable valid inter-subject comparisons while controlling for scanner differences across sites.
source: For each tissue compartment, site-specific average fiber response functions were calculated across participants (Raffelt et al., 2012b), which enable valid inter-subject comparisons while controlling for scanner differences across sites (Smith et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raffelt et al., 2012b and Smith et al., 2022.

claim: The FOD template was composed of 38 participants selected to be unbiased by sex and include representation from a wide range of ages and reading levels.
source: There were no females in the RD group among the two oldest age bins, so our template was composed of 38 participants. We implemented this method to make a robust high-quality template that was unbiased by sex and included representation from a wide range of ages and reading levels.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A whole-brain tractogram with 20 million streamlines was generated from the FOD template using seeds uniformly distributed across the template-space voxel-wise mask.
source: A whole-brain tractogram with 20 million streamlines was generated from the FOD template using seeds uniformly distributed across the template-space voxel-wise mask (Tournier et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: SIFT filtering was applied to account for false positives in streamline generation, resulting in a pruned tractogram with 2 million streamlines.
source: SIFT filtering (Smith et al., 2013) was applied to account for false positives in streamline generation (Maier-Hein et al., 2017), resulting in a pruned tractogram with 2 million streamlines.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: p-values were corrected across the brain using Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction.
source: p-values were corrected across the brain using Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Tract masks tended to overlap, so a single fixel could be associated with multiple fiber bundles.
source: We note that tract masks tended to overlap (Schilling et al., 2022), so a single fixel could be associated with multiple fiber bundles.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schilling et al., 2022.

claim: The study replicated recent studies suggesting that FA does not relate to reading skills.
source: In our secondary analyses, we replicated recent studies suggesting that FA does not relate to reading skills (Moreau et al., 2018; Koirala et al., 2021; Meisler and Gabrieli, 2022; Roy et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the secondary analysis results and citations to recent studies.

claim: Different manifestations of white matter plasticity from learning to read, such as axonal pruning and increased myelination, can have opposing effects on FA.
source: Different manifestations of white matter plasticity from learning to read, such as axonal pruning and increased myelination, can have opposing effects on FA (Yeatman et al., 2012), confounding FA analyses and their interpretations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yeatman et al., 2012.

claim: DWI signal is largely insensitive to myelination.
source: However, DWI signal is largely insensitive to myelination (Beaulieu, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beaulieu, 2002.

claim: Multimodal studies probing rapid intervention-driven changes have suggested that properties of myelin do not change throughout reading intervention.
source: Multimodal studies probing rapid intervention-driven changes have suggested that properties of myelin do not change throughout reading intervention (Huber et al., 2021), with mixed evidence for whether MD (which relates to extra-axonal properties) tracks intervention responses (Huber et al., 2018; Partanen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huber et al., 2021, Huber et al., 2018, and Partanen et al., 2021.

claim: DWI alone cannot discern whether intra-axonal volume is driven by the number of axons or width of axons.
source: However, one should still interpret FDC findings cautiously. DWI alone cannot discern whether intra-axonal volume is driven by the number of axons or width of axons, and fixel-based metrics have not yet been validated against histological standards.
evidence: This claim is based on the limitations of DWI methodology.

claim: Fixel-based metrics have not yet been validated against histological standards.
source: However, one should still interpret FDC findings cautiously. DWI alone cannot discern whether intra-axonal volume is driven by the number of axons or width of axons, and fixel-based metrics have not yet been validated against histological standards.
evidence: This claim is based on the current state of validation for fixel-based metrics.

claim: Collapsing participants into reading proficiency groups loses information about individual differences in reading ability.
source: It is also important to consider that collapsing participants into reading proficiency groups loses information about individual differences in reading ability.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical reasoning about categorical vs. continuous analyses.

claim: Studies of pre-readers would help rule out concerns that findings are due to the consequences of developing typical or poor reading skills, as opposed to the etiology.
source: Studying pre-readers would help rule out concerns that findings are due to the consequences of developing typical or poor reading skills, as opposed to the etiology, which is a concern for studies of late-stage readers (Protopapas and Parrila, 2018; Protopapas and Parrila, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Protopapas and Parrila, 2018 and 2019.

claim: Other studies have found white matter microstructural alterations, largely in the left arcuate fasciculus, among pre-readers who have either a familial risk for dyslexia, lower pre-reading skills associated with risk for dyslexia, or future diagnoses of dyslexia.
source: There has not yet been a fixel-based analysis focusing on pre-reading skills, but other studies have found white matter microstructural alterations, largely in the left arcuate fasciculus, among pre-readers who have either a familial risk for dyslexia, lower pre-reading skills associated with risk for dyslexia, or future diagnoses of dyslexia (Saygin et al., 2013; Vanderauwera et al., 2015; Vandermosten et al., 2015; Langer et al., 2017; Vanderauwera et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on pre-readers.

claim: Areas where ODI negatively related with reading skills approximately overlapped with where FD positively related with reading abilities.
source: Interestingly, in the present results, areas where ODI negatively related with reading skills approximately overlapped with where FD positively with reading abilities (Figure 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the ODI and FD analysis results shown in the figures.

claim: Most participants in the HBN present with at least one psychological, learning, or neurodevelopmental disorder.
source: Secondly, most participants in the HBN present with at least one psychological, learning, or neurodevelopmental disorder (Alexander et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alexander et al., 2017.

claim: The study did not exclude participants based on the presence of other neurodevelopmental or learning disorders such as ADHD or specific language impairments to maintain high statistical power and a diverse sample.
source: To maintain high statistical power and a diverse sample, we did not exclude participants based on the presence of other neurodevelopmental or learning disorders such as ADHD or specific language impairments.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the discussion section.

claim: White matter bundles can have different shapes across participants.
source: Further, since white matter bundles can have different shapes across participants (Yeatman et al., 2011; Wassermann et al., 2011) and analyses are performed in a single template space, an effect in a region of fixels could be partially driven by global geometric variations across participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yeatman et al., 2011 and Wassermann et al., 2011.

claim: The study is cross-sectional and correlational, and thus cannot be used to make causal conclusions of white matter's contributions to reading skills.
source: Finally, we reemphasize that our study is cross-sectional and correlational. Thus, it cannot be used to make causal conclusions of white matter's contributions to reading skills.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the discussion section.
